findings: [prose-quality] “He counts the quarter-turns of the valve before the smell gets through to him.” -> “He counts the quarter-turns of the valve before the smell reaches him.” : NEW at fleet-repair-1, edits[1], q1 option B. The old wording ended on the bare definite “the funnel”, which is the tic the edit was sent to remove; the replacement trades it for an idiom clash. Get through to somebody is a phrasal verb about making contact or being understood, not about a smell arriving at a nose, and this is the one option in the set where a learner has to picture the physical act. Reaches him keeps the definite gone, keeps the collocation right, and stays clear of the key's catches the smell, so no new lexical echo is created inside the set.

[prose-quality] “and slow gas gives up more than fast gas, which on a new estate makes it worse” -> “and slow gas gives up more than fast gas, and on a new estate the gas is slow” : carried from round 1 vote 1 and re-filed, because the sentence it sits in is the one that lists the three factors and Q3 is the item that asks a reader to weigh them. Which has no clausal antecedent that makes anything worse, it has none at all, and the load-bearing step - a new estate draws little, so the gas is slow - is left for the reader to supply in the middle of a three-term list.

[prose-quality] “the twenty-six houses above it are due to be lit on Thursday” -> “the twenty-six houses above the vessel are due to be lit on Thursday” : carried from round 1 vote 1, and the cost doubled at fleet-repair-1. One sentence binds it twice to two referents - the bottom of it is the lane, above it is the vessel - and the new Q5 C limb, edits[9], now reprints the whole span as a citation, so the re-bind is read twice instead of once. The identical string inside the Q5 C limb must move with the passage or byte-identity fails.

findings: [correctness] “with the heavy dose fitted into the weeks in front of it” -> “with the heavy dose fitted into the weeks before it” : NEW at fleet-repair-1, edits[9], the Q5 A limb. Option A reads “It stands, because the heavy dose was fitted into the weeks before the houses were due”, so the limb has to restate BEFORE the date before it refutes anything. In front of runs the other way in time in English - the weeks in front of a date are the weeks still to come - so as written the limb restates a proposition option A does not make and then refutes that. The refutation itself is sound and does not move; only the restatement points the wrong way.

findings: [prose-quality] “and the slot decides nothing on its own; three of the four then sit in that frame without strain” -> “but only three of the four then sit in that frame without strain” : NEW at fleet-repair-1, edits[0], the gap-1 limb. JUDGEMENT ON THE REJECTED ROUND-1 WORDING, which the coordinator asked for: fleet-repair-1 was RIGHT to reject it. Round 1 prescribed “Nowadays is not, because a present-time adverb will not sit on had lived” under the heading that three of the four are grammatical and one is not. “Nowadays, they had lived there eleven years” is syntactically well formed; what fails is temporal deixis against a past perfect, which is a semantic clash and not ungrammaticality - compare Recently, they had lived there eleven years, which is fine on the same frame. Calling the string ungrammatical would have taught a learner that a sentence-initial adverb plus past perfect is a syntax error, which is a second false claim about English in the same limb that the first one was being removed from. The adopted diagnosis (it puts the time in the present while the verb after the gap is in the past perfect) is accurate, and the scoping of the conclusion to “Among the three that do sit there” is exactly the repair the finding actually wanted. The round-1 correctness defect on this unit is discharged; what is left is the seam above.

The one student-facing edit fleet-repair-1 made here - the stem, edits[0] - reads clean aloud, is grammatical, and introduces no defect I can find: the two stacked possessives (Jerrowsett's reason for going past her meter's curve) are heavy but idiomatic, the according-to-the-text frame does not strand the key (D is a paraphrase of a directly quoted span), and the frame's four new content words - according, text, reason, going - appear in no option, so the lexical-echo picture is exactly what it was: A alone echoes meter and curve. JUDGEMENT ON A ROUND-1 FINDING I AM NOT ESCALATING: “A small instrument loses more to the stiffness of its wire than the figure allows for.” and its echo “Short thick wire does lose more to stiffness” describe inharmonicity as a loss when the effect is that partials run sharp. That is a wrong-headed metaphor and round 1 was right to notice it, but it stays PROSE-QUALITY and I do not prescribe an edit, for two reasons: the metaphor is defensible as forfeiting the arithmetic rather than losing energy (the passage itself frames it as the further out they go), and the same rationale states the true direction explicitly in its closing paragraph - a stiff string's partials sit above the whole-number multiples rather than below them - so no learner is left holding the wrong picture. Escalating it would force an option edit, a whole-set form re-screen and a refutation re-derivation for a defect that costs nobody an answer. The other three round-1 findings (the bare elliptical upright, the it that shifts inside one speech turn) are recoverable and are not re-filed.

findings: [prose-quality] “A is put together from two places in the essay that are never brought together.” -> “A is right, and it is assembled from two places in the essay that are never brought together.” : carried from round 1 vote 2, where it was filed and then carried unrepaired. The host copula has no stop of its own and no colon to license the borrowed one, so the sentence is terminated only by the full stop that belongs inside the quotation. [prose-quality] “He gave up the circuit in 1903” -> “Inglebeck gave up the circuit in 1903” : carried from round 1 vote 1. He reaches back over nine intervening sentences, not one of which contains a human referent - they are mileages, markets, charters and coaches. In a 200-word passage that has deliberately turned itself into a gazetteer, the reader has lost the man by the time the pronoun arrives, and this is the sentence that closes the essay.
justification: Read aloud, passage and all four limbs with two sentences either side, then the one repaired string twice. The essay's trick - print the card, then let the market days arrive out of order two sentences apart so the reader has to sort them - is well made, and the mileages are exact (nine to Nerresby, thirty on to Thrapmere of which twenty-one lie beyond Haddenthorpe: 9 + 21 = 30). The one student-facing edit fleet-repair-1 made, edits[0] in the D limb, reads clean aloud and introduces nothing: “Nerresby is nine miles from Haddenthorpe against Thrapmere at twenty-one” is elliptical in the ordinary comparative way, states only distances the passage gives, and asserts no ranking. JUDGEMENT ON THE REJECTED ROUND-1 WORDING: fleet-repair-1 was RIGHT to reject “Nerresby is the nearer of the two other market towns, nine miles out”. Four places on this card hold markets - Haddenthorpe by the 1227 charter, Nerresby on Tuesday, Thrapmere on Wednesday, Lower Shenwold on Thursday - so from Haddenthorpe there are three other market towns and not two, and this rationale's own A limb calls all four of them towns, which closes off the narrower reading in which towns means only the three the coach road served. My round-1 wording would indeed have swapped one false geographical claim for another, and the neutral two-distance restatement the lane wrote instead is better than what I prescribed. Nothing in the unit teaches against its own key.

Option B turns on precisely which places the road served, so a learner who reads the four towns and then the three towns has been handed a reason to think the road served four. Places is neutral, costs nothing and leaves the B limb's argument intact.
